content: The risk of developing dental caries will increase as the population of the country ages. Older adults often require multiple medications to manage chronic health conditions, and many of these medications can lead to a reduction in salivary flow, which is a known risk factor for caries. Consuming drinking water with an optimal concentration of fluoride can help mitigate the risk of caries in older adults. Research has demonstrated that the prevalence of root caries among adults is inversely associated with the fluoride concentration in community drinking water. In other words, higher fluoride levels in drinking water are linked to lower rates of root caries. Water fluoridation has also been shown to reduce disparities in caries prevalence between children from low-income families and those from higher-income families. Individuals from lower socioeconomic status (SES) groups experience significantly higher rates of dental caries compared to those from higher SES groups. The reasons for this discrepancy are not fully understood, but it is hypothesized that individuals in lower SES groups may have less knowledge about oral diseases, reduced access to dental care, lower adherence to recommended oral hygiene practices, or may be harder to reach through traditional public health initiatives and private dental care systems. As a result, individuals from lower SES groups may derive greater benefit from fluoridated community water compared to those from higher SES groups. Regardless of socioeconomic status, water fluoridation remains the most effective and efficient public health strategy for reducing the prevalence of dental caries.
